no_grade_a_sources: no first-party customer/prospect conversation, interview, call, on-site search, or AI-conversation corpus was supplied. All buyer-language evidence is public forum or search proxy and is graded B at best. Wording is therefore proxy language, not observed customer language of record.

conflict_price_cap_level: aggregator pages report the 1 July 2026 cap as GBP 1,862 (source-016); the Ofgem primary press release reports GBP 1,663 (source-004). Primary regulator source is preferred; the aggregator figure is retained as disputed counterevidence.

conflict_supplier_scores: aggregator summaries report an Octopus Which? customer score of 74% and an OVO low of 56% (source-016); the Which? article itself reports Octopus 79% and names British Gas, EDF and Scottish Power below 60% (source-007). Primary publisher preferred.

conflict_citizens_advice_rank: aggregator summaries assert the target 'ranks first' in Citizens Advice ratings; the Citizens Advice Q1 2026 table itself shows rank 4 of 13+ at 3.67/5 (source-006). Publisher table preferred.

unverified_grant_change: the claim that the Boiler Upgrade Scheme rises to GBP 9,000 for oil/LPG homes from 21 July 2026 (source-015) appears only on commercial aggregator pages and was not confirmed against gov.uk or Ofgem. Any cell depending on it is quarantined.

personal_data_excluded: the target home page displays first names and some full names of individual reviewers and support staff. These were deliberately not recorded here or in the contamination register because they are unnecessary personal data.
decay: source-007 fieldwork ran September-October 2025 and source-008 is dated March 2024. Both are used for direction and language shape, not for current pricing or current service quality.

retrieval_method: source-011, source-014, source-015, source-016 and source-017 were observed through search-result summaries rather than direct page retrieval. Their spans are faithful paraphrases of those summaries and carry lower confidence, recorded in span_locator.

sources.title: Octopus Energy home page
sources.span: Names the tariff and service set: Intelligent Octopus Go, Octopus Tracker, Agile Octopus, Intelligent Octopus Flux, Outgoing Octopus, Octopus Fan Club, Cosy heat pumps, solar panels and batteries, EV chargers from GBP 949, Electroverse, Octoplus rewards, salary sacrifice EV, business energy. Also asserts 'Which? Recommended Provider' for '9 years running', a 4.8-star review rating, 'most awarded energy supplier', and savings claims including 'save around GBP 370 a year' on heat pumps.
sources.span_locator: home page product navigation, tariff cards, award badges, hero copy

sources.title: Outgoing Octopus export tariffs
sources.span: Three export variants (Agile Outgoing, Outgoing at '12p per kWh', Prime Outgoing at '16p per kWh' 4pm-7pm and '9p per kWh the rest of the day'). Stated requirements: 'a smart meter from which we are able to receive half-hourly export data', an export MPAN from the network operator, being an import customer, pairing only with certain import tariffs, and not having started feed-in-tariff payments in the last 12 months.
sources.span_locator: tariff variant cards and eligibility list

sources.title: Octopus Energy heat pump explore page
sources.span: Names a 'Cosy' heat pump range, a median post-survey price of 'GBP 4,459, which is lower than the national average of GBP 5,600' after the 'GBP 7,500 Boiler Upgrade Scheme', and the 'Cosy Octopus tariff' and 'Flexible Octopus (standard variable) tariff'. States 'Actual savings vary depending on system design, tariff choice, home insulation, and energy use'. No property-suitability, radiator, cylinder or insulation preconditions are set out on this page.
sources.span_locator: pricing block, tariff references, savings footnote

sources.title: Energy price cap will rise by 13% from July
sources.span: Cap of 'GBP 1,663 per year' for a typical dual-fuel Direct Debit household from 1 July 2026, a 13% overall rise with electricity up about 5% and gas up about 24%. Advises that 'Consumers have a range of options to help reduce their energy bills, including switching or fixing their tariff' and urges anyone struggling to contact their supplier first. Notes direct debit can save about GBP 143 a year and that smart-meter customers may access discounted weekend electricity rates.

sources.title: Changes to energy price cap between 1 July and 30 September 2026
sources.span: Direct-debit averages inclusive of VAT: electricity 26.11p per kWh with a 57.19p daily standing charge; gas 7.33p per kWh with a 29.04p daily standing charge. States 'You are not affected by the changes to the energy price cap if you have changed to a fixed rate tariff.' Attributes the rise to higher wholesale gas prices. The next cap period (1 October to 31 December 2026) is to be published by 26 August 2026.
sources.span_locator: unit rate table, fixed-tariff note, next-announcement note

sources.title: Compare domestic energy suppliers' customer service (Q1 2026 star ratings)
sources.span: Table labelled 'Scores for January to March 2026'. Octopus Energy rank 4 at 3.67/5; E.ON Next rank 3 at 3.71/5; OVO rank 8 at 3.30/5; Scottish Power rank 10 at 2.94/5; EDF rank 11 at 2.90/5; British Gas rank 13 at 2.61/5.

sources.title: Revealed: the energy suppliers that top our rankings for 2026
sources.span: Survey of 11,945 energy customers, fieldwork September-October 2025. Recommended Providers: 100Green 82%, Octopus Energy 79% and 'for the ninth year in a row', E (Gas & Electricity) 78%, Sainsbury's Energy 76%. British Gas, EDF Energy and Scottish Power scored below 60%; British Gas 'received 0 out of 5 for switching practices'.
sources.span_locator: recommended provider list, low performer paragraph, methodology box

sources.title: Forum thread: half-hourly versus fixed overnight EV tariff with solar and battery
sources.span: Owner of an EV, solar, a house battery and a controllable charger asks 'Anyone with similar installation using Agile instead of Intelligent Go seeing advantage over the above?' and whether the half-hourly import tariff is 'compatible with the Outgoing 15/kwh tariff'. Replies compare the share of hours below the fixed overnight rate and raise battery round-trip losses.

sources.title: Forum thread: deemed export or smart export?
sources.span: Legacy feed-in-tariff solar owner with no export smart meter asks 'Could I do better though by switching to Smart Export Tariff?', 'is there a way I can calculate the difference between the two tariffs?', 'Is SEG a better return than deemed export?' and 'is there a difference in SEG payments between providers?'. Constraint: an existing guaranteed annual payment they do not want to lose, and a physical access limitation.

sources.title: Forum thread: smart meter, is it worth it?
sources.span: Household with an EV, solar on a legacy feed-in tariff and a mechanical meter says 'I'm still skeptical about them' while weighing whether a smart meter would unlock cheaper EV rates or better export payments. A reply raises that 'about 5% cannot connect and send data'.

sources.title: Forum discussion titles on direct debit increases while in credit
sources.span: Recurring user-written thread titles include 'Direct Debit Increase BUT in credit', 'E-on increasing my Direct Debit when in Credit', 'Energy accounts perpetually in credit' and 'Energy Direct Debit - Predicted to be in plus at FYE but they want to increase'. Explanations in the summaries describe suppliers annualising forecast cost, deducting credit and dividing by twelve, and customers objecting to held credit balances.
sources.span_locator: search-index thread titles; individual threads not directly retrieved

sources.title: Is it time to fix your energy or stay on the Price Cap?
sources.span: Updated 24 July 2026. Names current alternatives against the cap: E.on Next Fixed 24m Exclusive v4 (8.2% below cap), E.on Next Fixed 12m Exclusive v5 (7.5% below), So Energy So Hawk 18m (4% below), So Energy trackers, Home Energy Fair Variable (16% below), E.on Next Smart Saver, EDF FreePhase Dynamic/Static, and the target's flexible, daily-wholesale and half-hourly tariffs. Consumer-facing question headings include 'Is it time to fix your energy or stay on the Price Cap?', 'How to check if it's worth fixing your energy', 'Prices have risen - is it worth fixing?' and 'What are the alternatives to fixing?'.

sources.title: Search-proxy query set: fixing versus staying on the price cap (July 2026)

Ranked results include 'Should I fix energy or stay on the price cap in July 2026?' and 'Best Time To Switch UK Energy Supplier Now (July 2026)'.

sources.title: Forum thread: Air Source Heat Pump - should I delay and hope costs fall?
sources.span: Thread title itself states the decision: whether to delay a heat pump and hope costs fall. Summary content lists the cost components homeowners itemise: the unit, a hot water cylinder, radiators, pipework, electrics, insulation and mounting, with whole-system quotes described from about GBP 5,000 to GBP 11,500 for a large property.
sources.span_locator: thread title and search-result summary; thread not directly retrieved

sources.title: Boiler Upgrade Scheme 2026 guidance (commercial aggregators)
sources.publisher: The Eco Experts and comparable commercial guides
sources.span: Multiple commercial guides state a GBP 7,500 Boiler Upgrade Scheme grant for air or ground source heat pumps in England and Wales, an EPC condition with no outstanding loft or cavity insulation recommendations, and a claimed increase to GBP 9,000 for oil or LPG homes from 21 July 2026. The GBP 9,000 change was not confirmed against a primary government source in this run.
sources.span_locator: search-result summaries for Boiler Upgrade Scheme 2026

sources.title: Disputed aggregator claims on cap level, survey scores and complaint rates
sources.span: Aggregator summaries variously state a July 2026 cap of GBP 1,862, an Octopus Which? score of 74%, that the target 'ranks first' in Citizens Advice ratings, and Ofgem Q2 2026 complaints of 14 per 10,000 customers against a 38 average. Each of these conflicts with, or is unconfirmed by, the primary publisher sources in this manifest. Retained as counterevidence only.

sources.title: Affiliate tariff comparison pages for smart EV and solar tariffs
sources.span: Affiliate comparisons describe a fixed six-hour overnight EV rate around 7p per kWh against a half-hourly wholesale-linked alternative, and argue the fixed overnight option suits drivers unless their car or charger is incompatible. Commercially motivated, target-adjacent, and not used here as a price fact.
